    Travel between Canada and other countries, May 2026

    Text - Selected Tables Related information Release schedule --

    Highlights

    In May, the number of Canadian-resident return trips from the United States increased 9.9% year over year, while trips to Canada by US residents jumped by 13.0%.

    Meanwhile, the number of Canadian-resident return trips from overseas rose 3.3% in May compared with the same month a year earlier, while trips to Canada by overseas residents increased 6.2%.

    Using seasonally adjusted data, the number of Canadian-resident return trips from abroad (from the United States and overseas countries) was up 1.0% in May, compared with April. The number of US-resident arrivals (+6.9%) and overseas-resident arrivals (+4.3%) also increased in May.

    Trips abroad by Canadian residents continue to increase

    Canadian-resident return trips from abroad rose 7.8% to 3.7 million in May, marking the second straight month of year-over-year increases.

    In May, Canadian residents returned from 2.6 million trips to the United States, representing a 9.9% year-over-year increase and the second consecutive month of growth following 15 consecutive months of year-over-year decreases. Nonetheless, the growth in May was boosted by a base-year effect, as the month showed a steep decline of 24.6% compared with May 2024.

    Canadian-resident return trips from the United States by automobile rose 17.7% compared with the same month a year earlier to 1.8 million in May 2026, with 65.5% of these being same-day trips. Return trips by air decreased 3.2% year over year to 703,700, while return trips by cruise ship increased 10.6% to 37,200.

    Canadian residents made 1.2 million return trips from overseas countries in May, up 3.3% year over year.

    Chart 1 
    Year-over-year change in the number of Canadian residents returning to Canada from trips abroad, May 2026

    Trips to Canada by United States residents continue to increase

    In May, US-resident trips to Canada totalled 2.2 million, rising 13.0% from the same month in 2025 and marking the fourth consecutive month of year-over-year increase.

    Arrivals by automobile (1.3 million) were up 13.6% year over year in May, with 52.6% of these arrivals being same-day trips, while arrivals by air increased 6.0% to 510,000. The number of US residents who disembarked in Canada from cruise ships rose 24.5% year over year to 244,900.

    Chart 2 
    Year-over-year change in the number of United States residents entering Canada, by province or territory of arrival, May 2026

    Trips to Canada by overseas residents increase

    In May, 665,300 overseas residents arrived in Canada, up 6.2% from the same month one year earlier. The majority (80.2%) of these arrivals were by air.

    By volume, arrivals from Europe (+31,000; +12.3%) and the Americas (excluding the United States) (+10,300; +12.1%) drove the year-over-year increase in overseas-resident arrivals in May, offsetting a decrease in arrivals from Asia (-9,800; -4.5%).

    In May, the top three countries of residence for overseas visitors were the United Kingdom, India and France, which together accounted for 30.2% of all overseas arrivals in Canada.

    Chart 3 
    Overseas visitors entering Canada, by continent of residence, January 2019 to May 2026

    Seasonally adjusted arrivals

    Tourism is influenced by seasonal and calendar effects. All statistics in this section are based on seasonally adjusted data (for more information, see the Note to readers).

    On a monthly basis, the number of Canadian-resident return trips from abroad was up 1.0% in May. Although Canadian residents made fewer return trips from overseas (-1.9%) in the month, this decrease was offset by an increase in return trips from the United States (+2.5%).

    Chart 4 
    Canadian residents returning to Canada and non-resident visitors entering Canada, January 2019 to May 2026, seasonally adjusted data

    The overall number of arrivals in Canada by US residents increased 6.9% on a monthly basis in May, driven by higher arrivals by automobile (+4.6%) and by other modes—like cruise ship, ferry and train (+32.6%).

    In May, the number of overseas-resident arrivals in Canada rose 4.3% on a monthly basis, driven by an increase in arrivals from Europe (+9.2%), Canada's largest overseas market. At the country level, the overall monthly gain was driven by higher numbers of visitors from the United Kingdom, Germany and Israel, offsetting the lower volume of visitors from India.

    Chart 5 
    Overseas visitors entering Canada, by continent of residence, January 2019 to May 2026, seasonally adjusted data

    Explore tourism data

    To further explore current and historical data in an interactive format, see the product Frontier Counts: Interactive Dashboard.

    For more current estimates of international arrivals to Canada, please see the release, "Leading indicator of international arrivals to Canada."

    For other tourism-related information, see the Travel and Tourism Statistics portal.

      Note to readers

    Unless otherwise specified, this release uses unadjusted (raw) data.

    For more information on concepts, definitions, data sources and methods, refer to Frontier Counts.

    Seasonal adjustment

    Tourism is influenced by seasonal effects (e.g., actual seasons and holidays such as Canada Day and Thanksgiving) and calendar effects (e.g., number of weekends in a month). Seasonally adjusted data are data that have been modified to eliminate the effect of seasonal and calendar influences to allow for more meaningful comparisons of economic conditions from period to period. For more information on seasonal adjustment, see Seasonal adjustment: Concepts and interpretation, 2026.

    Revisions

    Seasonally adjusted data for February to April 2026 have been revised. No revisions were made to the unadjusted data.

    Integrated Primary Inspection Line – Air integration

    In 2025, Statistics Canada integrated information about travellers processed through the Canada Border Services Agency's Integrated Primary Inspection Line – Air (IPIL Air) system into the Frontier Counts. Users are advised to exercise caution when comparing 2025 and 2026 reference months with previous years since published data before 2025 do not include IPIL Air.

item.text: The guessed `dq260723a` page is hanging and the `dq260723b` page is a travel release, so I won’t use either as evidence. The WDS vector is sufficient for the official numeric history and current level; I’ll avoid adding a narrative source unless I can fetch the exact EI release cleanly.

The latest official vector has data only through May 2026, so the August target is three unpublished monthly steps ahead. I’m computing the base rate on the last 24 values in thousands and successive monthly changes for the interval.

item.command:
/bin/bash -lc "python - <<'PY'
import json, urllib.request, statistics, math
req=urllib.request.Request('https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/wds/rest/getDataFromVectorsAndLatestNPeriods',data=b'[{\"vectorId\":64549350,\"latestN\":24}]',headers={'Content-Type':'application/json'})
data=json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req))
pts=data[0]['object']['vectorDataPoint']
vals=[(p['refPer'][:7], p['value']/1000, p['releaseTime']) for p in pts]
changes=[vals[i][1]-vals[i-1][1] for i in range(1,len(vals))]
print('last values')
for row in vals[-12:]: print(row)
print('changes last 23:', [round(x,2) for x in changes])
print('last 12 changes', [round(x,2) for x in changes[-12:]])
for n in [6,12,23]:
    ch=changes[-n:]
    print('n',n,'mean',round(statistics.mean(ch),3),'std sample',round(statistics.stdev(ch),3),'median',round(statistics.median(ch),3),'p10?',round(sorted(ch)[max(0,int(math.floor(0.1*(len(ch)-1))))],2),'p90?',round(sorted(ch)[int(math.ceil(0.9*(len(ch)-1)))],2))
print('values last24 mean',round(statistics.mean(v for _,v,_ in vals),2),'std',round(statistics.stdev(v for _,v,_ in vals),2),'min',min(v for _,v,_ in vals),'max',max(v for _,v,_ in vals))
last=vals[-1][1]
# persistence forecast 3-month ahead, interval sigma of monthly changes * sqrt(3)
sigma=statistics.stdev(changes[-12:])
hw=1.28*sigma*math.sqrt(3)
print('persistence point',last,'sigma12',sigma,'hw3',hw,'lo hi',last-hw,last+hw)
# drift forecast using mean last12 changes 3 months
mean12=statistics.mean(changes[-12:])
point=last+3*mean12
print('drift point',point,'lohi',point-hw,point+hw)
# last 6 drift
mean6=statistics.mean(changes[-6:]); sigma6=statistics.stdev(changes[-6:]); hw6=1.28*sigma6*math.sqrt(3)
print('mean6',mean6,'sigma6',sigma6,'point6',last+3*mean6,'hw6',hw6)
PY"

item.text: The strongest simple benchmark is last-print persistence at 543.69 thousand; the recent six-month drift is lower, but the 12- and 24-month history is not uniformly negative. I’m checking the latest official Labour Force Survey as a current signal before deciding whether to move materially away from persistence.

item.text: The July LFS is a direct current signal: employment up 75,000, unemployment down to 6.4%, and the unemployment rate down 0.5 points since April. That justifies a modest downward adjustment from persistence, but not adopting the full six-month drift because EI eligibility and administrative timing lag.
